also: have a tough time of it

terms.grammar: verb, first conjugation: with ex and the ablative of the part, or the ablative of the illness
evidence: Cic. Fam. 7.26.1: graviter ex intestīnīs labōrārem
terms.comment: Properly “toil, be in difficulty”. Of the part that hurts, ex: ex pedibus, ex rēnibus (Cic. Tusc. 2.60, Lewis & Short); of the illness, the ablative: gravēdine labōrāre, to have a cold (Traupman 56, 63).

terms.grammar: the passive of afficiō, with the ablative
evidence: Cic. Fam. 6.19: dolōribus pedum (Lewis & Short, s.v. afficiō)
terms.comment: dolōre afficī, to be in pain (Traupman 105, 152); morbō affectus, ill.

evidence: Cic. Tusc. 2.35: cum varicēs secābantur C. Mariō, dolēbat
terms.comment: See hurt. Cicero keeps the two verbs apart: aliud est dolēre, aliud labōrāre: Marius felt pain when his varicose veins were cut, and toiled when he led the march in great heat (Tusc. 2.35); there labōrāre is toil, not illness.

phrases.latin: Cum decimum jam diem graviter ex intestīnīs labōrārem
phrases.english: When I had been suffering badly with my stomach for ten days now

phrases.latin: dīxit tē in lectō esse, quod ex pedibus labōrārēs
phrases.english: he told me you were in bed because you were suffering with your feet
You’ve got a cold (literally, you are suffering from a cold).
to have a tough time of it

sources: Lewis & Short: laboro · Lewis & Short: afficio · Lewis & Short: doleo
